feedback: If a learner says the move 'adds a zero', agree the written numeral gains a zero (for whole numbers) but ask WHY: push for 'because its value became ten times bigger' so the idea still works for decimals later, where 'add a zero' breaks down.
If a learner says 3,000 is '10 more' than 300, build 300 with place-value counters and stack it ten times to reach 3,000, showing it is ten lots of 300, i.e. ten TIMES, not ten more.

Confirm correct answers by having the learner read both numbers aloud with place names (three hundred vs three thousand) so the VALUE, not just the digit, is heard — this also counters 'they're the same, both are 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
activities.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart

feedback: If a learner answers 'ten times' for a two-shift gap (50,000 vs 500), have them slide the digit place by place and count: one shift ×10, a second shift ×10 again, so ×100 in total.

If a learner gives a subtraction answer ('45,000 more' for 50,000 vs 5,000, or '49,500 more' for 50,000 vs 500), re-voice the question as scaling: 'how many of the smaller value fit into the larger?' and build with counters.
Praise answers that name both the factor and the reason (number of shifts), not just a number.
activities.intendedInsight: The factor between two placements of a digit equals ten raised to the number of column shifts: one shift is ×10, two shifts is ×100. Non-adjacent places are not automatically 'ten times'.
learnerActions: Compare the same digit in two different places, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000.
Slide one placement of the 5 towards the other, counting the number of column hops.
State the factor: one hop = ×10, so the 5 in 50,000 is ten times the 5 in 5,000.
Repeat for a non-adjacent pair, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500: count the hops (two), so the factor is ×10×10 = ×100.
Say in words how many times greater, and justify by the number of place-shifts.
activities.title: How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts

feedback: If a learner computes 700 ÷ 70 as something other than 10, have them see 700 as ten 70s on the chart (70 shifted one place left) before recomputing.
If a learner gets 10 but cannot explain it, ask them to point to where 70 and 700 sit and say how many columns apart they are.
Give full credit only when the sentence is linked to the place-shift, not just the correct number.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication sentences such as 700 ÷ 70 = 10 express the adjacent-place relationship itself: moving one place is ×10 or ÷10.
learnerActions: Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain the answer using place names, not just the computed digits.
Explain how 700 ÷ 70 = 10 connects to 70 and 700 sitting in adjacent place-value columns (the 7 in 700 is one place to the left of the 7 in 70, so 700 is ten times as much as 70).
Write a few matched pairs showing both directions, e.g. 30 = 3 × 10 and 3 = 30 ÷ 10.
Point to or highlight the two adjacent columns involved for each sentence so the quotient of 10 is seen as a single left/right place step.
activities.title: Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step

feedback: If a learner cannot say why 'ten more' fails, compute 300 + 10 = 310 and compare with 3,000, showing 'ten more' gives the wrong number.
Reinforce that the multiplicative view is what lets the ÷10 direction keep going into tenths and hundredths.
If the learner self-corrects confidently, extend by asking them to state the one-tenth (÷10) relationship: this place is one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Ten times' (multiplicative) and 'ten more' (additive) are different; place value is multiplicative, which is why the pattern extends consistently into decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim that 'the 3 in 3,000 is ten MORE than the 3 in 300' and decide whether it is right.
Explain why it is wrong and restate it correctly as 'ten TIMES'.
Support the correction with evidence: 300 × 10 = 3,000, or ten stacks of 300 reaching 3,000, or the single left-shift on the chart.
Preview the right-hand direction: a dimmed column to the right of the ones is where tenths will later live (the ÷10 direction continues past the ones).
activities.title: Ten times or ten more? Correcting the claim
